title: Three-dimensional Architecture of Basal Bodies and the Mastigont System in Trichomonas vaginalis
content: Trichomonas vaginalis is a parasite that is sexually transmitted (STI) that affects more than 156 million people worldwide and can lead to reproductive tract inflammation, adverse pregnancy outcomes, and an increased risk of HIV and other virus infections. In addition, it can provoke cervical and prostate cancer. T. vaginalis has five flagella, which emerge from the basal bodies as four anterior flagella and one recurrent flagellum. Many common and uncommon organelles are present in this parasite. The most peculiar and uncommon is the hydrogenosome, a producing ATP and molecular hydrogen organelle, and a complex and elaborate mastigont system which comprises the pelta-axostylar complex, formed by microtubules and the pelta that has a role of reinforcing the wall of the flagellar canal which is the flagellar exit [1]. In addition, several fibers, appendages, and rootlet filaments associated with the basal bodies form a poorly studied complex accessory system [2, 3]. The ultrastructure of the basal apparatus was analyzed in detail by UHR-SEM (ultra-high resolution scanning electron microscopy), tomography, immunofluorescence, immunolabeling, negative staining, and serial thin-section electron microscopy of isolated cytoskeletons. Analysis of extracted membrane cells with posterior SEM analysis revealed new rootlets fibrils, which were not seen in thin sections. Several new features are described, including those in the transitional region. The three-dimensional architecture of basal bodies and surrounding regions are presented. Gamma-tubulin was not detected in the accessory structure; however, anti-centrin antibody was found on the triplets and the lumen of the basal bodies with more intense labeling at its distal end. It was also localized adjacent to the triplets of the basal bodies [4].
